raw.answer: The case asked whether tax authorities may still investigate, demand extra tax, or penalize a taxpayer whose reported income was at or above the standard set for their line of business. The court said they may if the taxpayer hid, under-reported or omitted income, and that the Ministry of Finance rules carrying this out do not conflict with the Constitution. However, the court said some wording in those rules could easily be misunderstood and should be reviewed and revised.
raw.held: Reporting income at or above the industry standard does not free a taxpayer from the duty to report honestly, so authorities may still investigate, collect extra tax or penalize for concealed, under-reported or omitted income. The Finance Ministry's inspection rules and 1970 order are not unconstitutional in this respect, but certain provisions are easily misread and should be reviewed and revised.

points.text: The rule that an original report at or above the industry standard is accepted was meant to simplify tax collection and make things convenient for both tax offices and taxpayers.
That rule does not mean taxpayers reporting at or above the standard are free of the duty to report honestly.
So if income was hidden, under-reported or omitted, authorities may still investigate tax information and demand extra tax or impose penalties under the laws the ruling names.
The Finance Ministry's spot-check measures, filing audit rules and 1970 order were made to carry out those laws, so they do not conflict with the Constitution in this respect.

However, those provisions refer to examining and spot-checking those who reached the standard and tell offices to adjust mismatched items, so they could be misread as allowing adjustment by guesswork even with no facts suggesting tax evasion.
Because that wording is easily misunderstood against the income tax law's rule on accepting the original report, it should be reviewed and revised.

who: Taxpayers who file income tax returns
Businesses filing profit-seeking enterprise income tax returns

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the Physicians Act that fines people who advertise medical services without a valid physician qualification is unconstitutional. The court decided it is not in conflict with the constitutional articles named in the ruling. It reasoned that the rule only bans unqualified people from advertising work that belongs to physicians, and does not stop denture-fitting practitioners from advertising their own work.
raw.held: Article 28-1 of the Physicians Act, which fines those without a valid physician qualification who place medical advertisements, does not conflict with Articles 15, 22, 23 and 152 of the Constitution.

points.text: Denture-fitting practitioners may only do denture fitting and repair, and may not do oral surgery or treat dental disease. Preventing and treating gum disease belongs to dentists.
If such a practitioner posts a dental sign advertising treatment of gum disease or tooth decay, that goes beyond their permitted work and counts as a medical advertisement belonging to physicians.

The state aims to protect public health and avoid delaying patients' access to proper care, so it bars physicians from improper advertising and fines unqualified people who run medical advertisements.

The fine rule only bans unqualified people from advertising physician work. It does not restrict signs for denture-fitting work, so it does not harm their work opportunities and does not conflict with the named constitutional articles.

who: People without a valid physician qualification

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance letter from 1977 was unconstitutional. The letter said land set aside as public facility reserve land before the 1973 urban planning law amendment, but inherited after that amendment, does not get the bigger 70% land value increment tax reduction when expropriated. The court held that the letter is constitutional.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance letter is consistent with the purpose of the law, does not violate the principle that taxes must be set by law or the principle of fairness, and does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: When the state expropriates private land for public projects, owners who sacrifice their rights for the public good get compensation and, where appropriate, fair tax relief. The land tax law and the Equalization of Land Rights Act provide a 40% reduction, and 70% for certain reserve land not transferred since the 1973 amendment.

Land value increment is usually figured from the announced current value at expropriation minus the original assessed value or the value at the previous transfer. For inherited land, the value at the start of the inheritance counts as the previous transfer value.
The 70% reduction is for land not transferred since the 1973 amendment, because a long time has passed and the gap between values is large.

Inheritance is a transfer exempt from land value increment tax, and the gap between values is generally smaller, so the tax burden is already lighter. Applying the 70% reduction as well would be unfair.
The Ministry treated inheritance as a kind of land transfer, matching the idea of a change of owner, so its letter follows the law's purpose and does not conflict with the Constitution.

who: Owners of public facility reserve land whose land was expropriated
Heirs who inherited such land after the 1973 amendment
Tax authorities applying the land value increment tax

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Taiwan Province rule violates the Constitution. The rule says that when a school does not renew a teacher's expired contract, it must list the teacher, give the reasons, and report to the education authority. The court decided the rule does not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: Article 52 of the 1978 Taiwan Province school staff hiring rules, which requires schools to submit a list with reasons to the education authority when they do not renew a teacher's contract, does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: The rule only sets out the procedure a school follows when it does not renew an expired teacher contract: list the names, state the reasons, and report to the supervising education authority.
The reporting requirement is meant to push schools to handle non-renewals carefully.
So the rule does not conflict with Articles 15 and 165 of the Constitution, which protect people's right to survival and the livelihood of educators.

Two Provincial Education Department letters were not what the final court judgment relied on, so they do not meet the requirements for requesting an interpretation and raise no constitutional question.

who: Teachers whose contracts expire without renewal
Education authorities that receive the reports

raw.answer: The case asked when the time limit for asking to reopen a civil case starts if the court's final decision relied on a legal view that the Judicial Yuan later interpreted as contrary to the true meaning of the law. The court decided the time limit runs from the day that interpretation is announced. But if the civil judgment became final more than five years ago, a reopening based on an obvious error in applying the law is still not allowed.
raw.held: The deadline to file for a retrial based on such an interpretation counts from the day the interpretation is announced, following the proviso of Article 500, paragraph 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. However, civil judgments final for over five years still cannot be reopened for an obvious error in applying the law, under Article 500, paragraph 3, and Interpretation No. 188 is supplemented.

points.text: The Judicial Yuan has the power to interpret the constitution and unify the interpretation of laws and orders under Article 78 of the Constitution.

If a final judgment's legal view is interpreted as contrary to the true meaning of the law, that interpretation can be used as a ground for retrial or extraordinary appeal, though not where the court's view was not an obvious error in applying the law.
Counting the filing deadline from the day the interpretation is announced is needed to protect people's rights.
An error in applying the law is a flaw of the original final judgment, so civil judgments final for over five years cannot be reopened on that ground, which keeps the legal order stable.

who: Parties to civil cases with final judgments

raw.answer: The case asked whether Article 12, paragraphs 2 and 3 of the Act Governing the Allocation of Government Revenues and Expenditures are unconstitutional. These provisions require half of the business tax and stamp tax revenue to be pooled and redistributed. The court decided they do not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: Article 12, paragraphs 2 and 3 of the revenue allocation law, which pool and redistribute business tax and stamp tax revenue, are consistent with Article 147 of the Constitution and do not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: The Constitution gives the central government the power to legislate and carry out the division of national, provincial and county taxes, and says poorer provinces and counties should get some aid to balance economic development.

The law makes business tax and stamp tax provincial and special municipality taxes, and requires 50% of total revenue to be pooled and distributed, by the province to its counties and cities or by the central government to provinces and special municipalities, in order to pool central and local finances for balanced local development.
Factories and mines are mostly in counties and cities within provinces, which raises local costs for education, health, transport, policing and other public services.
Because business tax can be paid where the head office is and head offices are mostly in special municipalities, the places hosting factories and mines receive less of these taxes.
Pooled distribution fairly adjusts income between provinces and cities so poorer areas can develop normally, which fits Article 147.

The provincial taxes in Article 109, paragraph 1, item 7 mean those already assigned to the province to distribute under the central government's division, so the provisions do not conflict with that article either.

who: Special municipalities (directly under the Executive Yuan)
Local governments hosting factories and mines

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Urban Road Act's procedure for removing or relocating existing obstructing buildings on planned road land is unconstitutional. The court decided it is not, because the Act requires compensation and lets affected people seek relief through appeals and administrative litigation. The ruling found no conflict with Articles 15 and 143 of the Constitution.
raw.held: The Urban Road Act's special procedure for handling obstructing buildings within road land, including Article 11, does not conflict with Articles 15 and 143 of the Constitution.

points.text: The Act exists to build, improve, maintain and manage urban roads, which serves the public interest. Privately owned land needed for roads may be expropriated under Article 10 as the law allows.

Article 11 sets a special procedure for old obstructing buildings: removal, relocation and compensation are planned together with the road plan. Owners are notified to remove or relocate only after the plan is finalized and announced, with at least three months' notice, and the authorities may carry out the removal if necessary.
The purpose of this procedure is to let road plans be completed quickly, so it is a special rule relative to Article 215 of the Land Act.
The Act still requires compensation, to be handled under the relevant laws and set at a reasonable and fair level, and it does not exclude other relevant laws on compensation and disputes.

Interested parties may file administrative appeals and administrative lawsuits against removal notices and compensation decisions, so people's rights are adequately protected and there is no conflict with Articles 15 and 143.

who: Owners of buildings obstructing planned urban roads
Owners of private land needed for roads
Road authorities carrying out road plans

raw.answer: The case asked whether civil servants who are dismissed or given demerit penalties can take their cases to the administrative court. The court decided that a dismissal directly affects the constitutional right to hold public office, so the dismissed official may seek court relief. A penalty of a major demerit does not change the person's status as an official, so denying court review for it does not violate the Constitution.
raw.held: A dismissal under the civil servant performance law or related rules directly affects the right to hold public office, so after the review procedures the official may bring an administrative lawsuit, and the listed earlier precedents no longer apply to that extent. A major demerit penalty and a superior's duty orders do not give a right to sue, and denying one is not unconstitutional.

points.text: Dismissals with a disciplinary nature are in substance disciplinary measures, and how that power and its remedies are set up should be reviewed and adjusted by the relevant bodies.

Whether a status-based administrative action can be challenged depends on its content; a dismissal directly affects the constitutionally protected right to hold public office, so the official may use the right to petition and sue under Article 16 and seek relief from a judicial body, until the relevant laws are amended.

An official who has used review and re-review (or similar procedures) is treated as having gone through the appeal stages, and under the principle that a right means a remedy may then sue in administrative court.
The earlier precedents barred all such appeals and lawsuits without distinguishing the content of the action, so they no longer apply where they conflict with this view.
A major demerit under the performance law does not change an official's status or directly affect the right to hold office, so barring lawsuits over it does not conflict with the Constitution.

A superior's duty orders within their supervisory scope, as dealt with in the 1951 precedent No. 19 on the civil servant service law, are not disadvantageous actions affecting status, so officials cannot sue over them and the precedent is not unconstitutional.

who: Public school teaching and administrative staff

raw.answer: This ruling dealt with three questions about Taiwan's administrative and patent law: whether rules making a patent-related act void when it misses a deadline are unconstitutional, whether a retrial can be sought when a final judgment overlooked important evidence, and whether a lawsuit to cancel an administrative act can go on after that act no longer exists. The court found the first two rules and practices not in conflict with the Constitution, and said the third is fine only in part: where a person still has a legal interest that could be restored by cancelling the act, the suit should be allowed.
raw.held: The patent deadline rules do not violate the Constitution, and neither do the court precedents refusing retrial on the civil-procedure evidence ground. The precedents on suits over vanished administrative acts are constitutional only in part, and should no longer be applied when the person still has a restorable legal interest.

points.text: The patent opposition process lets the public or interested parties have a published utility model re-examined, but it can be abused to delay applications, so acts missing the deadline are void to protect applicants.

The voidness rule does not block proper opposition, since a late party with a proper reason, as the patent office accepts, is excepted. It is needed to stop others from obstructing and to settle applications early, so it does not infringe litigation or property rights.

Grounds for retrial must be set out in law to protect the finality of judgments. The administrative litigation law omits the overlooked-important-evidence ground, which is a shortcoming, but the court must still weigh such evidence when it relates to a listed retrial ground.
Because of that, the precedents refusing to use the civil-procedure retrial ground in administrative cases are consistent with this view and do not conflict with the right to litigation.
A suit to cancel an administrative act presupposes that the act exists, so if it no longer exists there is no need to start or continue the suit. The precedents are constitutional to that extent.

If an act has lapsed through time or other causes but the person has a legal interest that cancelling it could restore, the suit should still be allowed, and the precedents should no longer be applied in that situation.

who: People seeking retrial of administrative judgments

raw.answer: The case asked whether members and speakers of provincial and municipal councils may also serve as principals of private schools. The court decided they may not, because the two jobs are incompatible. Those already holding both jobs when the ruling was published must give up one of them.
raw.held: Provincial and special municipality council members and speakers may not serve as private school principals. Anyone already holding both at the time of the ruling must resign from one of the two positions.

points.text: Whether an elected representative may hold another post depends on whether the Constitution or a law consistent with it forbids it, or whether the post's nature is compatible with the representative's duties.
Earlier rulings on the Control Yuan, National Assembly and Legislative Yuan were based on this same approach.
A private school principal runs the school under the law, carries out board decisions and is supervised by the education authority. The job is heavy and needs full attention.
The private school law says principals must work full-time and may not hold other posts, except teaching at their own school, in order to keep schools well run.
Provincial and municipal council members are people's representatives with heavy duties, and speakers have even more, such as running council affairs and chairing meetings.
Holding both roles would distract the person, harm school affairs and blur lines of responsibility, so the roles are incompatible.

who: Those holding both posts before the ruling

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Customs Anti-Smuggling Act rule is constitutional. The rule lets customs require a deposit or guarantee before it will hear an objection to a penalty or tax recovery. The court held that Article 49 does not conflict with the constitutional guarantees of equality (Article 7) and the right to bring claims (Article 16), but said the appeals procedures should be reviewed and improved.
raw.held: Article 49 of the Customs Anti-Smuggling Act is not in conflict with Articles 7 and 16 of the Constitution. The court also said the Act's administrative appeal procedures are not fully thought through and should be reviewed and revised.

points.text: Equality under Article 7 means substantive equality in legal standing. It does not stop the law from letting an authority make reasonable, different decisions based on real differences between cases and the law's purpose.
Article 49 gives customs discretion to look carefully at each case and decide whether to require a deposit or guarantee. It does not mean customs may demand one whether or not it is needed.
The purpose is to stop people from raising objections without good reason in order to delay or avoid paying duties and fines.

The rule limits a person's chances of relief, but it targets only those with no seized goods, or too little seized, to cover the fine or tax, and where the original decision is not clearly unlawful or improper.
Because it is necessary to carry out anti-smuggling policy and advance the public interest, it does not conflict with Articles 7 and 16.

If a person appeals a customs demand for a deposit, the appeal body or administrative court must review whether the demand was lawful and appropriate. A superior agency may act if the original decision was clearly unlawful or improper.
The appeal procedures in the Act are not fully thought through and can lead to errors in enforcement. They should be revised to balance securing enforcement with people's right to appeal and sue.

who: People penalized by customs who object

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Ministry of Finance's directive was unconstitutional. It said that when individuals sold a house and could not prove the actual sale price and original cost, their gain was always counted as 20% of the house's assessed value. The court held that estimating income is allowed, but this fixed-percentage method is unfair and does not match the income tax law's intent, so it must stop being applied within six months.
raw.held: The Ministry's directives setting the gain at a flat 20% of the assessed value must stop being applied within six months of the ruling's announcement.

points.text: The Constitution says people must pay taxes according to law, and taxpayers must file their own returns and show books and documents proving their income so the tax authority can check them.

If a taxpayer does not file or does not show proof, the tax authority may set the income from the information it finds or from industry profit standards. The court said this estimating method does not conflict with the Constitution.
Any such estimate must be objective and reasonable and based on experience, so it is close to the taxpayer's actual income and keeps taxation fair.
The flat 20% rule applies the same fixed percentage of assessed value regardless of year, region or economic conditions, so it is hard to bring close to reality and is unfair and unreasonable.
The court also said the flat rule does not aim to find the true facts of each case, and does not fully fit the intent of the income tax law on estimated income.
A separate Taiwan Provincial Tax Bureau letter was already covered by the Ministry's directives, so it needed no separate interpretation.

who: Individuals who sold houses without proof of price and cost

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule requiring tax to be paid on shipping containers that are not sent back out of the country on time is unconstitutional. The court decided the rule is not unconstitutional. A container that is not re-exported in time can be taxed by charging the carrier or its agent who held it when it was imported.
raw.held: Article 16 of the Customs Container Management Measures, which was revised and issued by the Ministry of Finance on 16 October 1976, does not conflict with the tax-by-law principle in Article 19 of the Constitution. Customs duty may be charged to the carrier or its agent who held the container at import if it is not re-exported within the time limit.

points.text: A container used to hold goods and imported apart from a ship is no longer ship equipment. If the tariff in force at import makes it dutiable, it is exempt only if re-exported within six months or by a date the Ministry of Finance sets.

The Customs Act says the taxpayer is the consignee, or the holder of the bill of lading or of the goods. The court relied on this together with the re-export exemption provision, both cited by article number in the ruling.

Article 16 requires the carrier or its agent to give customs an annual container guarantee to re-export within six months or the set date. If they do not, they must pay the import duty within three months. This follows the meaning of the two Customs Act provisions and matches international container customs practice.
Charging the carrier or its agent who held the container at import therefore does not conflict with the tax-by-law principle in Article 19 of the Constitution.
The Ministry of Finance's 1983 letter was not the rule applied in the final judgment, and its content is already covered by the container measures, so the court only noted this.

raw.answer: The case asked whether government orders barring new credit cooperatives in townships and placing their management under the financial authorities were unconstitutional. The court held that credit cooperatives do banking-type business, so they are financial institutions subject to state management, and the orders do not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: The Executive Yuan's 1964 order that credit cooperatives may not be newly set up in townships, and the Ministry of Finance's 1970 interim rules on entrusted unified management, do not conflict with Articles 14 and 145(2) of the Constitution.

points.text: Credit cooperatives lend money and take deposits, which are banking business, so they are financial enterprises that must be managed by the state according to law, as Article 149 of the Constitution provides.
Freedom of association (Article 14) and state encouragement of cooperatives (Article 145, paragraph 2) are recognized, but they do not displace lawful state management of financial institutions.

The Banking Act (Articles 26 and 29) allows limits on adding banks in certain areas and bars non-banks from banking business, and the Cooperative Act (Articles 5 and 10) limits deposits from non-members and lets the authority approve or refuse a cooperative's setup.
The Executive Yuan and Ministry of Finance acted under their legal powers and authorization, considering actual social, economic and financial needs, to manage financial institutions.
The court added that setup conditions and management matters should be reviewed and adjusted as social, economic and financial conditions change.

who: People wanting to set up credit cooperatives in townships
Financial authorities (Executive Yuan, Ministry of Finance)

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Act for Collecting Public Works Benefit Fees makes these fees something that must be collected or only something that may be collected. The court decided they must be collected when a project meets the legal requirements. Local representative bodies reviewing a collection plan may still check whether the requirements are met.
raw.held: Under Article 2 of the Act, benefit fees for projects that meet the collection requirements are to be collected, with a stated minimum amount. Local representative bodies reviewing the plan under Article 5 may also examine whether the requirements are met, and Article 22(1) of the Fiscal Revenue and Expenditure Division Act does not turn the fees into optional ones.

points.text: It is fair for those who directly benefit from a public works project to share its cost, and the Act follows this idea.

Article 2 of the Act makes the fee one to be collected for projects where the government builds or improves a specific public work with direct beneficiaries, and it sets a minimum amount, so qualifying projects must be charged.

Local governments must draw up a collection plan (project plan, budget, benefit area, fee rate) and send it to the representative body for a decision, then report it to the higher-level government for the record.

When a local representative body reviews the plan under Article 5, it may also examine whether the collection requirements are met; if the plan is delayed or rejected, the project's budget should be delayed or cancelled too.

Article 22(1) of the Fiscal Revenue and Expenditure Division Act only means benefit fees may be used as a source of revenue, with related legislation to collect them, so it does not make the Act's fees optional.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a court can treat a person who reported a crime (the 告發人) as a witness and use the Code of Criminal Procedure's rules to compel attendance. The court said yes. A reporter is a third party to the case, so if the court thinks it needs their testimony, it can summon them, and if they fail to appear without a proper reason, it can have them brought in to testify.
raw.held: A person who reported a crime is a third party outside the case, so a court that finds it necessary may summon them as a witness under Article 178 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and may have them brought in by force if they do not appear without proper reason. Earlier Interpretation No. 47 applying this to reporters does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: A witness is a third party who states what they saw or heard at the court's order. This information is key to finding the truth and cannot be replaced.
Except where the law makes special exceptions, anyone has a duty to testify in court proceedings.

Article 178, paragraph 1 allows a fine and compelled attendance for witnesses who are properly summoned and do not appear without proper reason, so that questioning witnesses can uncover the truth. This is necessary to maintain social order and promote the public interest.
A reporter is a third party to the case, so when the court finds it necessary to have them state what they know, it may treat them as a witness under that rule.
Interpretation No. 47, which allowed this rule to be applied to reporters, does not conflict with the Constitution.

raw.answer: The case asked whether it is unconstitutional for provincial and municipal audit offices to audit the agencies under their provincial or city governments. The court decided it is not, because auditing is a central-government power under the Constitution's five-branch system. The audit offices belong to the central Audit Department under the Control Yuan.
raw.held: The Audit Department, which is under the Control Yuan, may set up audit offices in provinces and municipalities. Those offices may audit the finances of the provincial or city governments and their agencies under Audit Act Article 5, and this does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: Under the five-branch system, the Control Yuan holds the audit power, and matters the Constitution assigns to the central government are legislated and carried out by the center (Articles 90 and 107, item 13).
Since auditing is a central power, the Audit Department's organization law lets it set up audit offices in each province and municipality to handle audits of those governments and their agencies.

Audit Act Article 5 gives provincial and municipal audit offices the audit of those governments' finances. This builds a unified audit system under the center, which is needed to oversee how provincial and city budgets are carried out.
Constitution Article 111 covers only matters not listed in Articles 107 to 110. Auditing is already assigned to the center, so Article 111 does not apply.

How centrally set-up audit bodies relate to local representative bodies reviewing final accounts should be set by a separate law under Final Accounts Act Article 31. Until then the current Final Accounts Act applies by analogy, and the authorities should enact a local final accounts law at a suitable time.

who: Provincial and municipal governments and their agencies
Audit Department and its local audit offices
Local representative bodies reviewing final accounts

raw.answer: The case was about whether civil servants who retire and claim a pension can challenge disputes over it through administrative appeals or lawsuits. The court said they can, as it had already explained in Interpretation No. 187. It also said a part of an earlier Administrative Court precedent that was worded too broadly lost its effect where it conflicts with that view.
raw.held: Civil servants who retire under the law and claim a pension may file an administrative appeal or administrative lawsuit. The first part of Administrative Court precedent No. 229 (1964) lost effect, to the extent it conflicts with Interpretation No. 187, once that interpretation was published. The part on military personnel's discharge applications is outside this interpretation.

points.text: Retiring under the law and claiming a pension is exercising a right that the law grants based on the Constitution, so the right deserves protection.
Because of that, disputes over it may, in procedure, be taken to an administrative appeal or administrative lawsuit, as Interpretation No. 187 already explained.

The precedent's statement that civil servants cannot file administrative appeals over administrative actions against them as civil servants did not distinguish between kinds of actions, so its meaning was too broad.
The conflicting part of that precedent therefore lost effect automatically after Interpretation No. 187 was published, under Interpretation No. 185.
The precedent's part on military personnel applying for discharge does not concern civil servants' pension claims, so it is unrelated to this request and not covered.

who: Civil servants subject to administrative actions

raw.answer: The case asked whether a guarantor (surety) can be a criminal offender under Article 38 of the Secured Transactions in Movables Act, which punishes a debtor who unlawfully disposes of the secured goods. The court decided that the offense applies only to the debtor in the secured transaction, not to the guarantor. A guarantor can be treated as an accomplice only if they acted together with the debtor or incited or helped the debtor.
raw.held: The Article 38 offense has the debtor in the secured transaction as its offender and does not include the guarantor.

points.text: Secured transactions must be made in writing with required terms, and who the debtor is follows from what these contracts record.

A guarantee contract is a secondary contract between a third party and the creditor and has no required form. The guarantor's debt depends on the main debt, so the guarantor's position differs from the debtor's.

Article 38 expressly names the debtor as the offender, and unlike Articles 39 or 40 it does not also list third parties. So it is an offense arising from the specific debtor relationship, and guarantors are not included.

A guarantor who acts jointly with the debtor, or incites or helps the debtor, is treated as an accomplice under Article 31, paragraph 1 of the Criminal Code. Otherwise a guarantor cannot be the sole offender.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a person who commits a new crime after an earlier judgment has become final can have the new prison term and the earlier one combined into a total of more than 20 years. The court said yes: the earlier and later fixed-term sentences are served together, and the 20-year cap does not apply. It also said that people who serve such combined terms and show real remorse should not face tougher parole conditions than people serving life sentences, and that this should be written into law.
raw.held: When someone receives a fixed-term prison sentence for a crime committed after an earlier judgment became final, the earlier and later terms are served together and the 20-year limit in Article 51, item 5 does not apply. Parole conditions for such a person who shows real remorse should not be stricter than for life imprisonment, and the court said a law should say so.

points.text: The 20-year cap in Article 51, item 5 applies only to setting a combined sentence for multiple crimes that were all committed before a judgment became final.

A crime committed after a judgment becomes final falls outside the multiple-crimes rules (as the court said in Interpretation No. 98), so the new sentence is added to the earlier one and the cap does not apply.

Otherwise someone sentenced to 20 years could keep committing crimes carrying prison terms without having to serve more time, which would breach the principle of one crime, one punishment, and would weaken protection of legal interests, public order and fairness.

The 20-year limit in Article 33, item 3 only restricts increases to the penalty for a single crime in substance or in treatment, so it has nothing to do with combined sentences for later crimes; the earlier interpretation (院字第626號) on this point can no longer be applied.

A fixed-term sentence is lighter than life imprisonment, so to serve the aim of rehabilitation, parole conditions for those with real remorse should not be stricter than for life terms, and the law should say so.

who: People who commit a new crime after a final judgment
Prisoners seeking parole after showing real remorse

raw.answer: The case asked whether an earlier Administrative Court precedent was unconstitutional. That precedent said a legal opinion cannot count as a 'piece of evidence' for reopening a final judgment. The court found it did not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: The Administrative Court precedent (1966 ruling no. 36) holding that a legal view is not 'evidence' under the old Civil Procedure Code Article 492, paragraph 1, item 11, and so cannot ground a retrial suit, does not conflict with the Constitution. The court also noted that later amendments made a final judgment's clearly wrong application of law a ground for retrial.

points.text: A retrial suit challenges a final judgment, so it should be reasonably limited to protect the stability of the legal order.
The precedent's main point is that a legal opinion differs from physical evidence based on the existence or state of things, so it cannot be used as newly found evidence to seek a retrial.
The precedent does not bar retrial suits based on the legally recognized grounds, so it does not conflict with the Constitution.
Amendments to the Civil Procedure Code (Feb. 1, 1968) and the Administrative Litigation Act (Dec. 12, 1975) later made a final judgment's clearly wrong application of law a ground for retrial.

who: People seeking to reopen final judgments
Parties to administrative and civil cases

raw.answer: The case asked whether rules that leave certain allowances out of the salary base used for retirement insurance, and that do not pay them to people who are not on duty, are unconstitutional. The court decided they are not. It said the rules stay within the discretion given by law and do not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: The rules that exclude work allowances, military duty extras and chief-officer bonuses from the retirement insurance salary base, and that withhold allowances from people not on duty, do not conflict with the Constitution. The same goes for the Executive Yuan letter saying suspended staff get no work allowance while suspended.

points.text: Civil servants have a right to claim retirement pay and insurance old-age benefits, but the benefit level is a matter of legislative policy and must be set by law or by orders the law authorizes.

The law authorized the relevant bodies to set these amounts: the Civil Service Retirement Act gave the Examination Yuan and Executive Yuan power over other cash payments, and the insurance law's rules and the salary law's delegations covered the rest.

The Executive Yuan's 1981 payment measures, which exclude certain allowances from the insurance salary base and do not pay people not on duty, were made by weighing state finances, whether someone is on duty, and insurance premiums paid. They can be adjusted with the economy.
Because of this, the rules did not go beyond the discretion given by the legislature or by its delegation, so they do not conflict with the Constitution.
The Executive Yuan letter that excludes work allowances for suspended staff reflects that such allowances are paid because of actual work, so it also does not conflict with the Constitution.

who: Staff suspended because of a case

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's tax collection law is unconstitutional in requiring people to pay a set share of the tax, or put up security, before they can ask for a review (復查) of a tax decision. The court found these rules unfairly limit people's rights to appeal and sue, and are unfair in how they delay enforcement. It gave the government up to two years to revise them.
raw.held: The rules making review depend on paying part of the tax or giving security, and delaying enforcement until the appeal process ends, conflict with Articles 7, 16 and 19 of the Constitution. They lose effect no later than two years after the ruling is published, and in the meantime must be reviewed and revised as a whole.

points.text: People who cannot pay the required share of tax or give security lose any chance at administrative remedies, so only those with money can use them. This is an unnecessary limit on the rights to appeal and sue.

Because enforcement waits until review, appeal or court proceedings are finished, people who applied for review can use the process to delay paying the rest or hide assets, so the rules do not even prevent the abuses they aim at.

The rule delaying enforcement is unfair to people who did not go through the remedy process, and it conflicts with the principle that starting a remedy does not stop enforcement of the original decision.

The rules therefore conflict with Articles 7, 16 and 19 of the Constitution and lose effect within two years, during which they should be revised together with tax preservation and priority-payment issues.

who: Taxpayers who cannot pay the required share or give security
Taxpayers who did not use the remedy process

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Taiwan Province tobacco and liquor monopoly regulation still applied to Kaohsiung after it became a special municipality in 1979. The court decided that it does, because the area the law covered has not been changed through the legal process. The court also said the law's name no longer matches its area, so the authorities should review and fix it.
raw.held: The 1953 temporary regulation on tobacco and liquor monopoly within Taiwan covered the Taiwan Province counties and cities, including Kaohsiung, at that time. Until that coverage is changed by the lawful procedure, it continues to apply to Kaohsiung after its reorganization.

points.text: The regulation was made to apply to the counties and cities of Taiwan Province at that time, and Kaohsiung City was among them.
Kaohsiung's change to a special municipality on 1 July 1979 did not change the area the law covers, and the area has not been changed by the lawful procedure, so the regulation still applies.

The Executive Yuan's reorganization principles say central laws named 'Taiwan Province' or 'within Taiwan' keep applying in Kaohsiung. For this regulation, that matches the law's original intent and does not conflict with Article 15 of the Central Regulations Standard Act.
Because the administrative boundaries changed, the law's name no longer fits its area. The court said the relevant agencies should promptly review and amend it so name and substance match.

who: Tobacco and liquor businesses in Kaohsiung

raw.answer: The case asked whether people may file an administrative appeal (訴願) against an agency's mere statement of facts or explanation of reasons, and whether barring this violates the constitution. The court held that the Administrative Court's precedent saying such appeals are not allowed simply interprets the Appeals Act and does not conflict with Article 16 of the Constitution.
raw.held: The Administrative Court precedent (62 Cai No. 41), which says an agency's plain statement of facts or explanation of reasons is not an administrative disposition and cannot be appealed, does not conflict with Article 16 of the Constitution.

points.text: Article 16 guarantees the right to appeal and sue, but administrative disputes must still follow the relevant laws.
Under Articles 1 and 2 of the Appeals Act, an appeal requires an administrative disposition (or something treated as one), meaning an agency act on a specific matter that has public-law effect.
The Administrative Litigation Act likewise requires an administrative disposition and an appeal procedure before suing, which matches the common approach of countries with similar systems.
A mere statement of facts or explanation of reasons does not grant or deny a person's request and creates no legal effect, so it is not an administrative disposition and cannot be appealed.

The precedent is the natural interpretation of the Appeals Act, does not go against Interpretation No. 156, and does not limit rights people are entitled to under the Act, so it does not conflict with Article 16.

who: People who want to file administrative appeals

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule allowing authorities to replace the manager of a temple that was built by public fundraising, when the temple delays or fails to register, is unconstitutional. The court decided the rule is consistent with the Constitution's protection of property rights. It said the rule matches the intent of the Temple Supervision Act and is needed to protect temple property and the public interest.
raw.held: Article 11 of the Temple Registration Rules, which lets authorities replace a temple's manager, is held not to conflict with constitutional property protection when applied to temples built by fundraising. The ruling covers only such temples.

points.text: Under the Temple Supervision Act, temple property and ritual objects must be registered, and a person who manages a temple must be a Republic of China citizen. Breaking these rules lets the authorities remove the head (住持).
A temple manager who is not a monk or Taoist priest, or who does not use the title of head, can still be covered if they actually have management authority over the temple.

The Ministry of the Interior made the Registration Rules under its lawful powers. Article 11 allows forced registration and, absent special reasons, replacement of the head or manager of a temple that delays or fails to register.

For fundraised temples, this rule fits the intent of the Temple Supervision Act and is necessary to protect temple property and promote the public interest, so it does not conflict with constitutional property protection.
The ruling covers only temples built by fundraising, and other temples are outside it. Replacement after removal was already dealt with in an earlier interpretation (院字第一七八八號).

who: Managers and heads of fundraised temples
Fundraised temples that have not registered

raw.answer: The case asked whether the placement rules for the 1983 special civil service exam for retired military personnel were unconstitutional. The rules limited placement of Grade B passers to officers and did not reassign people already placed in jobs. The court found these rules did not conflict with the constitution's guarantees of equality and the right to take exams and hold public office.
raw.held: The placement rules in the exam notice did not violate the constitutional guarantees of equality or the right to take exams and hold public office. Limiting placement to officers, even though the Grade B exam also admitted noncommissioned officers and placement did not follow exam rankings, was not entirely appropriate but did not raise a constitutional problem.

points.text: The constitution's equality, including equality in the right to take exams and hold public office, means substantive equality, so appropriate legal limits made for real practical needs and the exam's purpose do not breach it.

The exam was held at the request of the veterans' assistance commission to meet a special practical need and to place retired and discharged service members in jobs in an set order, under the relevant laws and rules.

The commission could set a placement order based on expected retirements and its capacity to place people, so the officer-only placement and no reassignment of those already placed followed the employment rules set by the responsible authority.

The rules let passers within the original placement plan get jobs, while others still gained eligibility to be appointed or promoted later, so they did not conflict with the constitutional guarantees.
Placing only officers, though noncommissioned officers could also take the Grade B exam and placement ignored exam rank, was not entirely appropriate but raised no constitutional problem.

who: Officers who passed the Grade B exam
Noncommissioned officers who took the exam

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance directive on how tax offices figure out interest income from mortgage-secured loans is unconstitutional. The directive lets tax offices use land registration records of the mortgage to calculate the lender's interest income, and puts the burden on the lender to prove no interest was received. The court decided the directive does not violate the Constitution.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance's 1983 directive is not contrary to Articles 15 and 19 of the Constitution, because it only guides tax offices on how to find the facts and does not bar a taxpayer from presenting contrary evidence.

points.text: Article 19's duty to pay taxes according to law covers who pays, what is taxed, the rate, the method and the period; whether a taxable fact exists and how strong evidence is are questions of fact, outside that principle.
The directive is an instruction to tax offices on how they themselves determine the facts behind a tax, not a rule on the elements of taxation.
The directive does not forbid parties from offering contrary evidence, so a person claiming no interest was received can still try to show it.
Courts are not bound by the directive; they must weigh the whole argument and the evidence to decide what is true.
So it is hard to say it infringes people's rights, and it does not conflict with Articles 15 and 19, even if it may be less than fully appropriate in places.

who: Lenders holding mortgage-secured loans with stated interest

raw.answer: The case asked whether a court can order that a sentence may be converted to a fine when it overturns a prosecutor's refusal to allow that conversion. The court decided it can, when necessary. The court may do this in the same ruling that cancels the prosecutor's decision, or it may leave the matter for the prosecutor to reconsider.
raw.held: When a court finds an objection to a prosecutor's refusal to allow conversion of a sentence to a fine justified and cancels the refusal, the prosecutor may reconsider in line with the ruling. If necessary, the court may also order in the same ruling that conversion is allowed. This differs from the situations covered in the earlier interpretations numbered 2939 and 1387.

points.text: Whether conversion to a fine is allowed is normally the prosecutor's power to direct, but the law gives people a way to object to an improper direction in order to protect the sentenced person.
The law sends such objections to the court to decide and does not limit what the court's ruling may contain, so the court may also allow conversion in the ruling to provide a remedy.
This follows the same legal reasoning as the rule allowing a court to cancel or change a prosecutor's disposition.
The earlier interpretations stated that carrying out a judgment is the prosecutor's power and that whether conversion is allowed depends on the facts at the time of enforcement.
Those earlier interpretations are different from the objection procedure, where the court cancels the prosecutor's direction and may allow conversion at the same time.

raw.answer: The case asked whether the government could use an enforcement regulation and a Ministry of Finance letter to set which interest income is tax-exempt under the Statute for Encouragement of Investment. The court decided that doing so by regulation, when the statute simply said 'all kinds of interest', went against the constitutional principle that taxes must rest on law.
raw.held: The enforcement rules and the Ministry of Finance letter, which defined the scope of exempt interest and excluded interest on private loans, conflict with the statute's words 'all kinds of interest'. They therefore violate Article 19 of the Constitution, even if they fit the aim of encouraging investment.

points.text: Under Article 19 of the Constitution, people pay tax according to law, which covers both what is taxed and what is exempt; both must be set out clearly in a statute.
Enforcement rules may only deal with matters of carrying out the parent law; where tax or exemption scope is involved, the law itself must decide it.

The statute exempted 'all kinds of interest' except postal savings and short-term bills, and did not exclude private non-investment loan interest, yet the rules and letter excluded private loan interest.
Serving the goal of encouraging investment does not justify setting this by regulation when it conflicts with the statute's explicit wording.

The statute was later amended to list exempt interest and the rule was deleted, so the letter no longer applies, but the court still interpreted it because an earlier interpretation gives effect to the applicant's own case.

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Code of Criminal Procedure's rule letting a court extend a suspect's detention by ruling is unconstitutional. The court decided that the rule does not conflict with Article 8 of the Constitution. It also added that the court's extension ruling should be made known to the accused in time.
raw.held: Article 108, paragraph 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, on court rulings extending detention, does not conflict with Article 8 of the Constitution.

points.text: Article 8 of the Constitution protects personal freedom, and arrest or detention must follow legally set procedures by judicial or police authorities.

Article 108, paragraph 1 limits the length of detention to make those carrying out detention act carefully, and lets a court extend it by ruling before the period ends if continued detention is needed. This carries out the purpose of Article 8.

Article 8, paragraph 2 concerns arrest or detention by bodies other than courts, so it does not cover a court ruling extending detention. Therefore a court's detention does not raise the issue of giving written notice and applying for a writ of habeas corpus.
To protect personal freedom, a court's extension ruling should be made known to the accused in time, following the relevant Code of Criminal Procedure provisions.

who: People detained on suspicion of a crime
Accused persons whose detention is extended

raw.answer: The case asked whether public land that joins a city land readjustment project needs approval from the Executive Yuan before it can be disposed of. The court decided it does not, because joining such a project is not the owner 'disposing' of the land under Article 25 of the Land Act. Article 25 therefore does not apply.
raw.held: When public land takes part in city land readjustment run by landowners' own readjustment association under Article 58 of the Equalization of Land Rights Act, it is not a disposition by the owner's own will, so Article 25 of the Land Act does not apply.

points.text: Readjustment can be carried out by authorities with higher-level approval, or by landowners forming their own association with the authority's approval. Public land may be mixed into either, and in substance both are the authority's administrative decision on whether to allow readjustment, meant to carry out the constitutional policy of equalizing land rights.
The landowners' 'consent' or 'objection' is only a way for private owners to prompt the authority to act or reconsider, and has nothing to do with public land.
The exchange and reallocation of land after readjustment is an effect set by law (Article 62), not a disposition made by the owner's own will.
'Disposition' in Article 25 of the Land Act means an act changing rights based on the owner's own will, so it does not include joining city land readjustment.
The Article 25 requirement of 'Executive Yuan approval' also differs from readjustment, where central or local authorities give approval under the Act.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the Civil Procedure Code is unconstitutional. The rule says a party living outside the court's location gets travel time added to legal deadlines, except when a litigation agent lives where the court is and can act within the deadline. The court decided that this exception does not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: The exception in Article 162, paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Code makes the actual deadlines for litigation acts the same for parties. It does not affect the exercise of the right to sue, and it does not conflict with Constitution Articles 16 and 23.

points.text: The right to sue under Article 16 is a right to seek relief when one's rights are harmed, and Article 23 allows it to be limited by law when necessary for the public interest.
The appeal deadline in the Civil Procedure Code lets the rights and duties between the parties become settled once the deadline passes without a valid appeal.

If a party has an agent living at the court's location who has been specially authorized to appeal, that agent can decide whether to appeal within the fixed deadline after receiving the judgment, so no travel time is subtracted.
The aim is to make the actual deadlines the same for parties who live at different distances from the court or who may or may not have someone at the court's location able to act.
This is necessary for the public interest and does not affect the exercise of the right to sue, so it does not conflict with Articles 16 and 23.

who: Parties to civil lawsuits living away from the court
Litigation agents living where the court is located
Parties who have authorized such an agent

raw.answer: The case asked whether rules requiring a public company's financial reports to be audited jointly by accountants in a joint accounting firm, and setting conditions for forming such firms, violate the Constitution. The court decided they do not conflict with the Constitution. It also said the authorities should review whether a different rule for accountants who qualified through a review exam is still reasonable and necessary.
raw.held: Articles 2 and 4 of the 1983 audit-approval standards, which require joint audits by two or more accountants of a joint firm and set conditions for forming such firms, do not conflict with the Constitution. The court added that the different conditions for accountants who qualified by review exam should be reviewed by the authority or set by law.

points.text: The standards were issued under authority given by Article 37, paragraph 1 of the Securities and Exchange Act, so they are rules made on legal authorization.
The joint-audit and joint-firm rules aim to balance accountants' knowledge and experience, raise audit quality and strengthen public trust.
These rules make the system for auditing public companies' financial reports sounder and fit the purpose of the authorizing law.
They are necessary to protect investors and advance the public interest, so they do not conflict with the Constitution.

Because years have passed, social and securities conditions keep changing, and the accountant review rules were amended, it is unclear whether the different conditions for review-exam accountants remain reasonable and necessary; the authority should review them or set them by law.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in Taiwan's Code of Civil Procedure is unconstitutional because it makes a plaintiff who withdraws a lawsuit still pay the court costs. The court decided the rule does not conflict with Article 15 of the Constitution. It reasoned that civil suits are for the parties' own private interests, so the party who starts the case should bear the costs it causes.
raw.held: Article 83, paragraph 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which says that when a plaintiff withdraws a suit the plaintiff bears the litigation costs, does not conflict with Article 15 of the Constitution.

points.text: A civil suit is a process in which parties ask the courts to settle their private rights, so paying the costs it creates is a requirement for filing and the plaintiff who withdraws must bear the costs of filing.
Because parties bring civil suits for their own benefit, it is fair for them to bear the resulting costs, so Taiwan's civil procedure law charges for court use and requires a fixed court fee to file.
If the fee is not paid after the presiding judge sets a deadline to fix it, the court must dismiss the suit by ruling.
When a court issues a final judgment, it assigns costs to the losing party or whoever caused pointless litigation, but a case does not always end in a judgment.

A plaintiff who withdraws before final judgment can file again, so making the plaintiff bear the costs helps prevent abusive filing; the court found this necessary for the public interest and not in conflict with Article 15.

who: Plaintiffs in civil lawsuits who withdraw their suits

raw.answer: The case asked whether two civil procedure rules violate the constitution: the limit on litigation aid for cases with obviously no hope of winning, and the time limit for asking to resume a case after a court settlement. The court held that both rules are consistent with Article 16 of the Constitution.
raw.held: The proviso in Article 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which denies litigation aid where the party obviously has no hope of winning, does not conflict with Article 16 of the Constitution. Article 380, paragraph 3, which applies the fixed period for retrial suits to requests to resume a case after settlement, also does not conflict with it.

points.text: Parties to a civil case should bear its costs, so the system charges fees, while litigation aid lets people without means still exercise their right to sue or defend.
Aid is withheld where, judging by the party's own claims, the case obviously has no hope of winning, to avoid pointless proceedings and added burdens; this is necessary for the public interest.
A court settlement has the same effect as a final judgment and ends the case.
If a request to resume the case succeeds, the ended proceedings are revived and the settlement loses its effect once the court issues a new final ruling on the original case.
So a time limit is needed to keep the legal order stable and transactions secure, and applying the fixed retrial period to such requests follows this purpose.

who: People who cannot afford court costs

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance rule is unconstitutional that lets businesses receiving post-dated checks issue their uniform invoice on the date printed on the check. The court decided the rule does not conflict with Article 23 of the Constitution. It also declined to review a separate complaint about Article 44 of the Tax Collection Act.
raw.held: The rule letting businesses that receive post-dated checks issue the uniform invoice on the check's printed date is not in conflict with Article 23 of the Constitution.

points.text: A check is a payment instrument that can be used in place of cash. Once the date printed on it arrives, it is payable on sight.
Uniform invoices are issued on an accrual basis, generally at delivery, but payments received before delivery must be invoiced first. A check can serve as payment in that situation.

The rule was made with the interests of businesses receiving not-yet-due checks in mind, and it fits the purpose of Article 12, paragraph 1 of the Business Tax Act as it then stood, so it does not conflict with Article 23 of the Constitution.

The complaint about Article 44 of the Tax Collection Act was really a dispute over whether a late invoice broke that article and whether Article 48-1 applies. That is not a constitutional question and falls outside this interpretation.

who: Businesses that must issue uniform invoices

raw.answer: The case asked whether administrative orders that touch on legal views used in trials can be brought to the court for interpretation, and whether two old Ministry of Justice letters about auctioning imported goods with unpaid customs duties were constitutional. The court said judges are not bound by such orders, but if a judge cites one in a judgment, a party may ask for an interpretation. It also found the two letters consistent with the customs law and not in conflict with the constitutional protection of property.
raw.held: Judges are independent and not bound by administrative orders on legal views, but a party may request interpretation of an order a judge cited in a ruling. The letters requiring auction notices to state unpaid customs duties, with the buyer paying them before delivery, do not conflict with the constitution's protection of property.

points.text: Judges try cases independently under the law, so they may cite agencies' explanatory orders but can express different views and are not bound by them.
Orders from judicial administration bodies do not affect the exercise of judicial power, so they serve only as reference for judges and cannot direct how judges apply the law.
If a judge cites such an order in a judgment, a party may ask for an interpretation, so this request was accepted.

Under the customs law provisions cited, goods with unpaid duties cannot be transferred, so a security interest in them cannot cover the unpaid duties. A buyer at a forced sale who is not allowed to continue paying in installments or on account must pay the duties to get the goods.
The two letters match those customs law provisions and fall outside the article 55 paragraph 3 provision, which concerns duties paid out of other property with only priority over ordinary debts.
The letters do not harm holders of security interests and are needed to secure customs collection, so they do not conflict with the constitution's protection of property.

who: Holders of security interests in goods
Buyers at auctions of imported goods

raw.answer: The case asked whether speed limits set for Kinmen by the Kinmen War Zone Political Committee were unconstitutional. The court decided they were not. It said the limits on suburban roads, including a 40 km/h cap on other roads and military roads, were needed because of the special road conditions in a war zone and to keep traffic safe.
raw.held: The Kinmen limit that suburban roads, apart from those set at 60 or 50 km/h, and military roads may not exceed 40 km/h is necessary for war-zone road conditions and traffic safety, and does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: The road traffic safety rule on speed by signs lets traffic authorities adjust speeds on particular road sections to local conditions, and where there is no sign, the general limits apply.
The Kinmen committee's 40 km/h limit on other suburban roads and military roads falls within what that rule authorizes.
The limit was needed because of special war-zone road conditions and to keep traffic safe.
If signs had not yet been put up at the time, that is a question of whether the administrative measure was poorly handled, not a constitutional problem.

raw.answer: The case asked what the phrase "evidence that must be examined at the trial hearing under this law" means in Article 379, item 10 of the Criminal Procedure Law. The court said it means evidence that objectively forms the basis for the court's findings of fact and application of law. Failing to examine other evidence does not fall under that item.
raw.held: The phrase covers only evidence that objectively underlies the court's fact-finding and application of law; failing to examine it makes the judgment unlawful by definition. Failing to examine other evidence is outside that item, and if Article 380 bars a third-instance appeal on it, it cannot be a ground for an extraordinary appeal either.

points.text: An extraordinary appeal is a special remedy against final judgments that violated the law, to unify how the law is applied; apart from Article 394, the rules on third-instance appeals are not made to apply to it.
A violation of law in the case's proceedings can count as the original judgment violating the law where it clearly affects the judgment, as explained in Interpretation No. 181.

The evidence meant in Article 379, item 10 is evidence already present in the fact-finding trial and objectively the basis for the court's findings and application of law; the statute says failing to examine it makes the judgment unlawful.
Evidence that is not objectively such a basis need not be examined, which avoids delaying proceedings and harming the public interest, as Article 172 shows.
Failing to examine such evidence falls outside item 10; if Article 380 limits it so that no third-instance appeal is allowed, it cannot be a ground for an extraordinary appeal.

The 1940 joint-meeting resolution, that procedural violations not affecting the judgment cannot support an extraordinary appeal, is lawful on evidence and does not conflict with Interpretation No. 181. Whether a given failure to examine evidence falls under Article 380 is decided case by case.

who: The Prosecutor General of the Supreme Court

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule saying labor-management arbitration committee decisions could be enforced by the authorities, together with a court precedent treating those decisions as final, blocked people from seeking legal remedies. The court held that the rule does not limit people's right to bring lawsuits, because disputes can still be taken through legal procedures. It also held that the precedent, which treated every such decision as final and beyond challenge, does not match this reading and can no longer be used.
raw.held: Article 8 (first part) of the wartime labor dispute handling measures does not restrict the right to sue and does not conflict with the Constitution. The Administrative Court precedent No. 528 of 1971, which called these decisions final and not open to challenge, may no longer be applied.

points.text: The rule letting the authority enforce a decision means the administrative agency carries out enforcement under the law when a party does not comply; it is not a bar on challenges.
The decision of the committee is of the nature of an administrative disposition, and enforcement means execution by the agency under the administrative execution law.
The existence of administrative enforcement does not make every decision final regardless of the type of dispute; parties with a dispute may still seek remedy through legal procedures.
Because remedies remain available, Article 8 does not limit the right to sue and does not conflict with Article 16 of the Constitution, which protects that right.
The precedent No. 528 called these decisions final and not open to dispute, which is inconsistent with this interpretation, so it may no longer be relied on.

who: Parties to labor-management disputes decided by the arbitration committees

raw.answer: The case asked whether "clerical workers" (事務性工人) count as "workers" under the Factory Act's enforcement rules. The court decided they do, as long as they are hired by an employer, work at the factory's work site or business site, and earn wages. The definition is not limited to people doing manufacturing, processing, repair or dismantling.
raw.held: A "worker" means anyone hired who does work and earns wages, not only those in manufacturing, processing, repair or dismantling. Clerical workers hired by an employer and working at the factory's work or business site for wages are included.

points.text: The meaning of "worker" under the Factory Act has changed over time. An older 1932 enforcement rule defined it more strictly, as people directly doing or assisting production work.

The 1975 amendment widened the Act's reach by dropping the 30-worker minimum and applying it to all factories using power-driven machines. The old enforcement rule was repealed and the Ministry of the Interior was authorized to make new enforcement rules.
To carry out the amendment's purpose, the 1976 enforcement rules, modeled on the Labor Safety and Health Act, defined workers more broadly in Article 3 as those hired to work who earn wages.
So anyone hired by an employer who works at the factory's work site or business site (including an office) for wages counts, not just those in manufacturing, processing, repair or dismantling.
The Taiwan Province factory worker retirement rules, as amended in 1979, use the same definition in their Article 3, so clerical workers are included there too.

who: Factory workers covered by the retirement rules

raw.answer: The case asked whether Ministry of Finance rules that estimate a small business's sales by dividing its operating expenses by an expense rate, and then tax those sales, are unconstitutional. The court decided they are not. It found the method is simpler for small businesses, allows for regional differences, and lets a business opt for the ordinary calculation instead.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance's rules for assessing business tax on small businesses, which use the expense-restoration method (operating expenses divided by an expense rate) to estimate sales, do not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: The Constitution's Article 19 requires paying tax according to law but does not forbid laws that allow tax to be set by estimation in particular situations, as an earlier interpretation (No. 218) had explained.

The Business Tax Act, in its 1980 and 1985 versions, itself provided for assessing small businesses' tax by fixed determination, and left the assessment methods to the Ministry of Finance, so these were legal rules for estimated taxation.

The Ministry's successive rules were consistent and could be applied one after another, all using the expense-restoration formula to estimate sales and apply the legal tax rate, which simplifies tax procedures for small businesses.
The expense standards take regional economic conditions into account, because local tax authorities set grade tables by area or district and file them with the Ministry, so the estimates fit reality.
A small business that does not want this special method may apply to calculate its tax by the ordinary method, the same as other businesses, which is consistent with tax fairness.
The court declined to interpret Article 8 of the Uniform Invoice Prize Measures because no final court judgment had applied it.

raw.answer: The case asked how to decide whether expropriated land is being used according to the approved plan, which matters when former owners want their land back under Article 219 of the Land Act. The court held that this must be judged by looking at all the expropriated land as a whole, not piece by piece. It found that a court precedent and an Executive Yuan order applying this approach do not conflict with Article 15 of the Constitution.
raw.held: Whether land is used "according to the approved plan" or "actually used" must be judged on the whole of the expropriated land, based on its intended purpose, without splitting it up where clear facts show the parts are related. The precedent and the order following this approach do not violate Article 15 of the Constitution.

points.text: Property rights are protected by Article 15, but the state may expropriate land for public use as the Constitution's other provisions allow.

After expropriation, the user must use the land within a set time according to the approved plan, to prevent abuse of expropriation power and protect private landowners; Article 219 lets former owners take land back at the original price if this is not done.

"Not used according to the plan" or "not actually used" should be judged on all the expropriated land together, according to its purpose, and not split up where clear facts show the parts are related, which fits the purpose of public expropriation.
The cited precedent and Executive Yuan order follow this approach, so they do not conflict with Article 15.

Whether an expropriation met legal requirements or went beyond what was necessary, what counts as whole-plan use in a given case, and any time limit on reclaiming land are outside this interpretation.

who: Agencies or bodies that need expropriated land
Administrative courts and agencies applying Article 219

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the enforcement regulations of the Estate and Gift Tax Act is unconstitutional. The rule says that money borrowed, or sale proceeds received, while the deceased was too ill to manage affairs still counts as part of the taxable estate if the heirs cannot show how the money was used. The court decided the rule does not conflict with Article 19 of the Constitution.
raw.held: Article 13 of the enforcement rules does not add to the tax duties set by law and does not conflict with Article 19 of the Constitution. Whether a taxable estate exists in a given case is still decided by the normal allocation of the burden of proof between the tax authority and the taxpayer.

points.text: Article 19 of the Constitution requires people to pay tax according to law, and the Act taxes the whole estate of a person who dies leaving property.
The Act allows deduction of the deceased's unpaid debts from the estate, but only if they are certainly proven.
A person too ill to manage affairs would ordinarily find it hard to handle borrowed money or sale proceeds personally, so the heirs should show how the money was used.
This requirement guards against heirs hiding estate assets by borrowing or selling in the deceased's name.

The rule carries out the Act's Article 1 and Article 17(1)(8), balances the heirs' interests with accurate identification of the taxable estate, and is needed to prevent tax evasion and keep taxation fair, so it adds no new tax duty.
In individual cases, the tax authority or the taxpayer must each carry the burden of proof as the usual rules allocate it.

who: Estates of people who were seriously ill before death

raw.answer: The case asked who counts as a 'tenant of farmland' under Article 11 of the Equalization of Land Rights Act, which gives tenants a share of compensation when rented farmland is taken. The court decided that it means only natural persons who actually farm the rented land themselves, and cooperative farms. It also said court decisions made before this ruling that read the provision differently are not treated as clear errors that justify a retrial.
raw.held: The tenant entitled to one-third of the remaining compensation (after land value increment tax) is a natural person who rents farmland and actually farms it personally, or a cooperative farm. Earlier court views on the wording before this ruling are not a clear error in applying the law and cannot be a ground for retrial.

points.text: The provisions serve the constitutional policy of supporting owner-farmers and people who use land themselves, and protecting farmers' livelihoods.

Under Articles 11, 76 and 77, when rented farmland is expropriated, appropriated, or taken back for building use, one-third of the remaining compensation goes to the tenant, so tenants are not left without a livelihood and cooperative farmers are also protected.

So the 'tenant' in Article 11 means a natural person or cooperative farm renting farmland and actually farming it; it excludes those farming land not rented as farmland, or farmland tenants who do not farm it themselves.
Because the court only now set out this meaning, earlier court views on the wording are not clearly wrong applications of the law and cannot be grounds for a retrial.

who: Tenants who personally farm rented farmland
Owners or agencies that must pay the compensation
Parties to earlier court cases on this provision

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Negotiable Instruments Act's criminal penalty for writing a check without enough money in the account is unconstitutional. The court decided it is not. It admitted the rule has been misused to stretch credit improperly, but said that is a question of whether the rule is well designed, which falls within the legislature's discretion.
