raw.held: Article 141, paragraph 2 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, which sets criminal penalties for bad checks, stays within the legislature's discretion and does not conflict with Articles 15 and 22 of the Constitution.

points.text: A check is a payment instrument meant to be paid at once and works like cash. The law makes the issuer guarantee payment, and it punishes issuers who knowingly write checks beyond their funds, in order to protect circulation, actual payment and transaction safety.

Post-dated checks can still circulate, so the penalty also applies when one is not paid on its stated date. However, using criminal punishment to secure circulation can lead holders to ignore the issuer's credit, and the rule has been used to expand credit improperly.
That flaw only raises the question of whether the provision is well designed. It stays within legislative discretion and does not conflict with Articles 15 and 22 of the Constitution.

An issuer may raise defenses against the holder. If a criminal court convicts without examining whether such a defense bears on intent, that is a question of whether the judgment was proper, not of whether the provision is constitutional.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a second marriage can be annulled when a spouse was separated from the other by a major national upheaval. The court held that the bigamy ban and the annulment rule are constitutional in general. But applying the annulment rule to a later marriage that grew out of such separation and involved a long period of real shared life conflicts with the Constitution.
raw.held: The old Civil Code bans on bigamy (Art. 985) and the annulment rule (Art. 992) do not conflict with the Constitution. But using Art. 992 to annul a later marriage formed under national upheaval, with spouses separated and no prospect of reunion and a long real shared life, conflicts with Article 22 of the Constitution.

points.text: The bigamy ban and the annulment rule are meant to build a one-husband, one-wife marriage system, and the rule has no time limit so annulment can be sought at any time. This is necessary to keep social order and does not conflict with the Constitution.
Before the 1985 amendment, the Civil Code did not make bigamy void as the later Article 988 does, so an unannulled later marriage stayed valid.
Bigamy during a national upheaval, with spouses separated, unable to reunite, or without word of each other, involved unavoidable factors and differs from ordinary bigamy.

Annulling such a later marriage after a long real shared life would deny people a normal married life and seriously harm the couple, their relatives, family life and human relationships, which in turn harms social order. So it conflicts with Article 22.
The petitioner may file a retrial action following Interpretations No. 177 and No. 185.

who: People in a later marriage formed while separated from a spouse by national upheaval
The earlier spouses and relatives of such couples

raw.answer: The case asked whether the "total budget" in Article 164 of the Constitution, which sets minimum shares of spending for education, science and culture, includes special budgets. The court decided that it does not. It refers only to the total expenditure in the regular annual general budget.
raw.held: The "total budget" in Article 164 means the total expenditure listed when the government prepares its annual general budget. It does not include special budgets proposed because of emergencies or major events.

points.text: The "total budget" in Article 164 means the total expenditure listed in the annual general budget that governments prepare for ordinary administration.
The annual general budget is compiled each fiscal year from all revenue and expenditure and is done only once per fiscal year.
A special budget may be proposed outside the annual general budget only when one of the circumstances listed in Article 75 of the Budget Act applies.
Because a special budget is prepared specially to meet emergencies or major events, it is not part of the "total budget" mentioned in Article 164.

raw.answer: The case asked whether Article 13 of the State Compensation Act is unconstitutional. That article lets people seek state compensation from judges and prosecutors only when the official was finally convicted of a crime in office over the case they handled. The court held that it does not conflict with the Constitution, because it is a special rule that fits the nature of judging and prosecuting and stays within the legislature's discretion.
raw.held: Article 13 of the State Compensation Act is a special rule suited to the nature of judicial and prosecutorial work. It stays within the legislature's discretion and does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: Article 24 of the Constitution led to state compensation legislation, and the legislature may reasonably set the conditions for claims. Article 2 is the general rule on state liability, and Article 13 is a special rule for judges and prosecutors.

Judges and prosecutors decide facts and law based on their own convictions, so differing views and some errors are hard to avoid. The litigation system can correct them, and criminal cases also have a wrongful-detention compensation system.

To protect judicial independence and keep prosecution free from outside interference, such errors should be tolerated within reason. Parties should not be able to simply label them unlawful and claim compensation.

When an official is finally convicted of a crime in office over the case, the unlawful harm is clear and is more than an error of judgment. The state should then pay compensation, as the Constitution intends.

Equality under the Constitution allows reasonable differences in state liability based on differences in state organs' functions. Article 13 is necessary to protect judicial independence and prosecution free from interference, so it does not conflict with Articles 7, 16, 23 and 24.
